items.prompt: Define management.
items.canonical_answer: Management is the activity of getting a business’s objectives achieved through the work of other people. The syllabus divides that activity into four functions: planning, organising, directing and controlling.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only: the meaning must reach achieving the business’s objectives through the work of other people.
Naming the four functions is creditable, but the definition has to carry the meaning first. No example or evaluation required.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between the organising function and the directing function of management.
items.canonical_answer: Organising is arranging people, tasks, authority and resources before the work starts: deciding who does what, who reports to whom, what each part of the work is given, and which decisions are delegated. Directing is the day-to-day work of instructing, guiding and motivating those people once the arrangement is in place. Organising settles the structure; directing operates inside it. A business can be well organised and badly directed - the reporting lines are clear but nobody explains why a target has changed - and it can be well directed and badly organised, where an energetic manager keeps work moving that two people each believe is the other’s job.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the difference are required, not one side plus a definition.
Boundary: organising sets the arrangement of people and authority, directing operates within it day to day.
Reward the point that a business may do one of them well and the other badly.

items.prompt: Explain why controlling is treated as a separate management function from planning.
items.canonical_answer: Because the two do different jobs at different points in time. Planning decides what should happen and commits resources and a timescale to it. Controlling compares what actually happened with that plan and acts on the difference. Without the second, the first is only an intention: a business could set a target of 52 000 crates a month, produce 44 000, and never find out in time to correct anything. Keeping them separate also makes the dependence between them visible, because a plan stated without a figure and a date leaves controlling with nothing definite to compare against, which is why weak planning shows up months later as weak control.
marking_guidance: Reason: the answer must say why the two are treated separately, not only describe each of them.
The purpose of controlling is the comparison and the action taken on the difference, not the measurement alone.
Support the point with the relationship between them: what happens to control when the plan carries no measurable target.

items.prompt: Etosha Bottling planned to raise output from 40 000 crates a month to 52 000 by the end of June. It recruited twelve staff for an evening shift, appointed a shift supervisor and briefs that shift nightly, but it counts output only once a quarter. Explain which management function is weakest at Etosha and what the weakness costs the business.
items.canonical_answer: Controlling. Planning has been done - there is a figure, 52 000 crates, and a date, the end of June. Organising has been done - twelve staff recruited, a supervisor appointed. Directing has been done - the shift is briefed nightly. What is missing is the comparison: counting output once a quarter means a shortfall in week four is not seen until week thirteen. The cost is the nine weeks of production run at the lower rate before anyone investigates, and the loss of the cause as well as the number, because by the quarter end nobody remembers which nights ran short or why, so whatever was behind the shortfall is harder to find. It also breaks the loop back into planning: the June target cannot be revised on evidence the business does not yet have.
marking_guidance: Context: must use Etosha’s own facts - the figure and the date are in place, the quarterly count is not.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that a long gap between measurements delays the discovery of the shortfall and the discovery of its cause.
Conclusion: one function must be named as the weakest, with what its weakness costs this business.

items.prompt: Analyse how setting an objective as “improve output” rather than as a figure and a date weakens a business’s ability to control.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the objective is set with no measurable target and no deadline. Immediate effect: the controlling stage has nothing definite to compare actual output against, so almost any level of output can be presented as an improvement or as a disappointment depending on who is arguing. Mechanism: a manager who cannot say whether the business is behind cannot say when to intervene, so corrective action is taken late or not at all, and the argument about whether there is a problem consumes the time the action would have used. Measurable consequence: shortfalls run for longer before they are found, so more output is lost at the lower rate and more of the cause is forgotten by the time anyone looks for it. Effect on an objective: the business is less likely to meet its delivery commitments, which puts the customer relationship behind them at risk, and the next plan is built on evidence nobody in the business trusts.
marking_guidance: Condition: the objective carries no figure and no date.
Mechanism: the comparison at the heart of controlling has no benchmark, so intervention is late.
Consequence: the answer must reach a measurable effect - output lost, or shortfalls found later.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must end on a business objective or a named stakeholder, such as meeting delivery commitments to a customer.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between Fayol’s five functions and Mintzberg’s ten roles as descriptions of a manager’s job.
items.canonical_answer: They describe different things. Fayol’s functions are purposes: forecasting and planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling are the ends a manager’s work serves, set out prescriptively as what a manager ought to be doing. Mintzberg’s roles are forms: figurehead, leader, liaison, monitor, disseminator, spokesperson, entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator and negotiator are the shapes the work takes while it is being done, set out descriptively from observation. The same hour can be described correctly by both - an hour spent settling an argument between two shifts is the disturbance-handler role, and the purpose it serves is directing - which is why the two accounts are not rival answers to one question.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: purposes the work serves against forms the work takes, and prescription against description.
Reward the point that one hour can be described correctly by both accounts.

items.prompt: In two hours a branch manager reads the overnight sales and stock-out figures, tells the counter staff which lines are short, negotiates a credit for a delivery that arrived two pallets light, handles a customer complaint herself in front of her staff, and decides that the one spare trolley jack goes to goods-in rather than the yard. Explain what her morning shows about managerial work, using Mintzberg’s roles.
items.canonical_answer: Each activity is a different role: reading the figures is the monitor role, telling the counter staff is disseminator, agreeing the credit is negotiator and disturbance handler together, handling the complaint in front of staff is figurehead and leader, and assigning the trolley jack is resource allocator. Six roles in two hours, none of them lasting more than half an hour, and not one minute of it recognisable as planning. That is Mintzberg’s finding in miniature: managerial work is fragmented and largely reactive, and much of it is done by talking rather than by writing or analysing. It does not show that she is managing badly. It shows that the functions describe why the morning mattered, while the roles describe what it actually consisted of.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the manager’s own activities rather than a general account of Mintzberg.
Reasoning: each activity must be matched to a role, and the pattern drawn from it - short, interrupted, spoken.
Conclusion: must reach the point that fragmentation is ordinary managerial work rather than evidence of poor management.

items.prompt: Explain why Mintzberg’s account of what managers do looks so different from Fayol’s.
items.canonical_answer: Because the two were answering different questions from different evidence. Fayol set out what he believed a manager’s job ought to consist of, working from his own experience of running a mining and metals firm, so his account reads as an orderly list of purposes. Mintzberg watched managers through their working days and recorded what they actually did, so his account reads as ten roles performed in short bursts with frequent interruptions. The purposes Fayol named are still being served in Mintzberg’s picture; they are simply not visible as separate blocks of time, because one interrupted conversation can serve two of them at once.
marking_guidance: Reason: the difference follows from prescription against observation, not from one account being wrong.
The purpose of each account must be made clear - what a manager ought to do, against what managers were seen to do.
Reward the point that the functions are still being served inside Mintzberg’s picture.

items.prompt: Analyse how a manager who neglects the monitor and liaison roles may end up taking worse decisions.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the manager stops gathering information about what is happening inside and outside the business, and lets contacts outside the immediate chain of command lapse. Mechanism: the decisional roles run on information, so a resource allocator who does not know which section is short, and an entrepreneur who does not know what a competitor has changed, are deciding on stale facts. Without liaison contacts the manager also loses the informal early warning that a formal report gives later, or not at all. Consequence: decisions are taken later than they need to be and are more often wrong - stock ordered for a line that has stopped selling, a problem worked on from scratch that another branch has already solved. Effect on the business: avoidable cost and lost sales, and a manager who ends up in the disturbance-handler role full time because nothing is seen coming.
marking_guidance: Condition: the two information-gathering roles are dropped.
Mechanism: the decisional roles depend on the informational ones, which depend in turn on the interpersonal ones.
Consequence: must reach a measurable effect, such as decisions taken on stale information or a problem solved twice.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must end on the business - cost, sales, or the manager’s own time.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to apply the formula selling price minus variable cost to “the contribution of managers to business performance”?
items.canonical_answer: Because the word contribution is being used in its everyday sense here: the part managers play in producing the result. The costing term met in topic 5.4 is a money figure calculated per unit sold, and it belongs to a question about products, not about people. No selling price and no variable cost exist for a manager, so the formula has nothing to work on. The part managers play is judged instead through the routes by which management affects results, and through indicators such as labour turnover, output per worker, cost per unit and whether the objectives set were met.
marking_guidance: The answer must say why the belief is wrong, not only that it is: the word carries two unrelated senses in this syllabus.
Reward the point that the everyday sense is judged through indicators rather than through a formula.

items.prompt: Explain how managing staff so that fewer of them leave can lower a business’s cost per unit.
items.canonical_answer: The mechanism runs in two parts. First, each person who leaves has to be replaced, and replacing someone costs money directly: advertising, the manager’s time interviewing, and the below-normal output of a new worker during training. Fewer leavers means that spending is not incurred. Second, the staff who stay accumulate experience, and experienced workers tend to produce fewer defects and take less time per unit, so the same output absorbs fewer labour hours and less wasted material. Both parts push total cost down while output is unchanged, so cost per unit falls. How large the effect is depends on how expensive replacement is in that business, and on how much the work actually improves with experience.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: both routes must be explicit - the replacement cost avoided, and the productivity of experienced staff.
Because the effect works through total cost at unchanged output, the answer must reach cost per unit rather than stopping at a general saving.
Reward the condition that the size of the effect depends on replacement cost and on how much the work improves with experience.

items.prompt: A furniture workshop with 50 staff saw labour turnover fall from 34% to 18% a year after a change to its shift roster. It reckons each replacement costs it about N$6 500. Explain what those figures mean for the owner.
items.canonical_answer: Turnover of 34% on 50 staff is 17 people replaced in a year; 18% is 9 people. The difference is 17 - 9 = 8 fewer replacements, so at N$6 500 each the roster change is worth 8 x N$6 500 = N$52 000 a year. What that means for the owner is that a decision costing nothing to make has produced a saving the workshop keeps without selling another chair. Read against the workshop’s own earlier year, it is the clearest evidence available that the roster was the reason people were leaving. Two cautions go with it. The N$52 000 counts only replacement cost and not the value of what the eight who stayed already knew about the work, so it understates the gain. And 18% is one year’s figure compared with one year’s figure; a second year at that level would make the case considerably stronger.
marking_guidance: Comparison: the figures must be read against the workshop’s own earlier year rather than in isolation.
Interpretation: the answer must give the meaning of the figures for the owner’s decision, not only recompute them.
Both cautions are creditable - the saving is understated, and a single year is weak evidence.

context.situation: labour turnover before and after a roster change

items.prompt: Analyse how a manager’s decision to review output weekly rather than quarterly could affect a business’s ability to meet a customer contract.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the control cycle is shortened from thirteen weeks to one. Immediate effect: a shortfall against target becomes visible within days rather than at the quarter end. Mechanism: the cause is still recoverable while it is fresh, because the shift that ran short can say what went wrong, so a training gap or a machine fault is dealt with before it has run for three months; acting early also costs less, because there is still time in the quarter to make the output up. Measurable consequence: fewer weeks are run at the lower rate, so cumulative output stays nearer the target. Effect on an objective and a stakeholder: the business is more likely to deliver the contracted volume on time, which protects the contract and the cash it brings in. The chain depends on the reports being acted on: weekly measurement that nobody responds to changes the paperwork and nothing else.
marking_guidance: Condition: the control cycle is shortened from quarterly to weekly.
Mechanism: an early signal keeps the cause recoverable and leaves time in the period for correction.
Consequence: must reach a measurable effect on cumulative output.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must end on meeting the customer contract, and must carry the condition that measurement without action changes nothing.

items.prompt: A bakery in Rundu employs eleven people. Its owner bakes alongside the staff all day and settles problems as they arise, but sets no targets and reviews no figures. Explain which of the routes by which managers affect performance this bakery is losing, and what that costs it.
items.canonical_answer: It is losing direction and control. The owner is directing, since problems are settled as they arise, but nothing tells the staff which work counts, and nothing compares what happened with what should have happened. What that costs the bakery is that effort goes where the day pushes it rather than where the objective is: a morning spent on a small custom order while the standing supermarket order runs late is not visibly a mistake, because no target says which of them matters more. And because no figures are reviewed, a drift in waste, in loaves sold, or in the hours worked per batch is not seen until it is large enough to feel in the bank balance. With eleven people the owner can hold much of this in their head for a time; the loss shows as the bakery grows, or on the first day the owner is away.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the bakery’s own facts - eleven staff, an owner working alongside them, no targets and no figures reviewed.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that without objectives nothing ranks the work, and without figures nothing signals drift.
Conclusion: one or two named routes must be reached, with what their absence costs this business.

items.prompt: Evaluate the view that the performance of a small business depends more on the quality of its managers than on the conditions it trades in.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: over a single year, trading conditions usually matter more for a small business, but over several years the quality of its management is what decides whether it survives the bad conditions, and that is the more useful way to read the claim. Context: a small business has thin reserves and few products, so one external shock - a drought that cuts a farming customer’s spending, an exchange-rate movement that raises the price of imported stock, a competitor opening nearby - can move its results further in a year than any management decision would. Criterion: the decisive question is which factor the business can still act on. Conditions are given; management is the part that is chosen, and it is management that decides what reserves are held, how wide the customer base is, and how quickly a problem is spotted. Counterargument: the strongest case the other way is that good management is largely invisible in a boom and cannot save a business whose market has gone, and that one year’s figures cannot separate the manager’s share of a result from the market’s. Condition: the judgement changes with the time horizon and the size of the shock. Over one quarter the conditions dominate; over five years, two businesses in the same town facing the same conditions diverge, and the difference between them is where management shows.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain verdict is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the answer must be argued for a small business with thin reserves, not for business in general.
Criterion: the decisive test is which factor the business can still act on.
Counterargument: must address the strongest case the other way - that a manager’s share of a result cannot be separated from the market’s in a single year.
Condition: must name what changes the answer, such as the time horizon or the size of the shock.

items.prompt: Define management style.
items.canonical_answer: Management style is the way a manager takes decisions and deals with the people they manage - chiefly how much say those people have in a decision, and how closely their work is directed once it has been taken.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a management style and a management function.
items.canonical_answer: A function is one of the things a manager does - planning, organising, directing, controlling - and a manager of any style does all four. A style is how those things are done, and specifically how much of a decision the manager keeps and how closely the resulting work is directed. Two managers running the same department perform the same four functions and may perform them in wholly different styles: one sets the output target alone and announces it, the other works it out with the supervisors first. The function tells you which part of the job is being done; the style tells you how the people affected are treated while it is done.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: what a manager does against how a manager does it, with the decision-sharing dimension named.
Reward the point that a change of style removes none of the functions.

items.prompt: The owner of a 40-room lodge outside Otjiwarongo decides the holiday rota alone, decides fire and evacuation procedure alone, and asks the housekeeping team to work out the room-cleaning sequence for themselves. Explain what this shows about how a manager chooses a style.
items.canonical_answer: It shows the style being matched to the decision rather than to the business. Fire procedure is kept because the consequences of getting it wrong are severe and there is no time to consult once an emergency has begun. The cleaning sequence is handed over because the housekeeping team knows the rooms, the linen cycle and the guest turnaround better than the owner does, so their knowledge improves the decision and their having chosen it raises the chance it is followed as intended. The holiday rota sits between the two: it affects everybody and the owner keeps it, which is defensible where competing requests have to be refused and a manager is better placed to carry the unpopularity than the staff are. Three different styles in one lodge is not inconsistency. It is the four factors - urgency, staff knowledge, the consequences of error, and what the manager believes about the staff - producing different answers for different decisions.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the lodge’s own three decisions rather than a general account of the styles.
Reasoning: each decision must be tied to the factor that explains the style chosen for it.
Conclusion: must reach the point that varying the style by decision is deliberate rather than inconsistent.

items.prompt: Analyse what may happen when a manager who has always decided alone announces that the business will now be run democratically.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: staff who have never been consulted are suddenly asked to contribute, and the manager’s own habits are unchanged. Mechanism: people used to being told have no practice at offering an opinion and no evidence that disagreeing is safe, so the first meetings produce little; the manager, reading the silence as proof that consultation does not work here, takes the decision anyway. Consequence: the staff now have direct evidence that the consultation is for show, so they contribute less to the second attempt than they did to the first, and the business has spent meeting time to reach a decision it would have had without it. Effect on the business and its staff: trust in what management says falls, which makes any later change harder to introduce, and the knowledge the consultation was meant to reach stays where it was. The outcome is conditional on how the manager handles the first decision that goes against their own view, because visibly accepting one such decision is what makes the rest of the change credible.
marking_guidance: Condition: the change is announced to staff with no experience of being consulted.
Mechanism: silence is read as failure, the decision is taken anyway, and staff learn the consultation is not real.
Consequence: must reach an observable effect - less contribution at the second attempt, and time spent for no change of decision.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must end on the business or its staff, and must carry the condition that the first contested decision determines the outcome.

items.prompt: A construction firm in Walvis Bay uses one management style for every decision in every department. Evaluate whether it should keep doing so.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: it should not. One style across every decision is the wrong style for at least some of them, and the firm should keep what it has for safety-critical and urgent decisions while consulting on decisions where the site teams know more than the office does. Context: a construction firm carries both kinds of decision in one business - a scaffolding method where an error injures somebody, and a sequencing question where a foreman who has built the thing four times knows something the planner does not. Criterion: the decisive factor is how much the conditions vary within this firm. Where urgency, staff knowledge and the cost of an error differ sharply between decisions, one style cannot suit them all. Counterargument: the strongest case for keeping one style is consistency - staff know where they stand, and a manager who consults on some things and not others can look arbitrary or look as though favourites are being picked. That is answered by explaining the rule, not by abandoning it. Condition: the judgement depends on the firm being willing to say which decisions are open and which are not. Varying the style without explaining why would be worse than either consistent style.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required.
Context: the answer must be argued for a construction firm carrying both safety-critical and knowledge-dependent decisions.
Criterion: the decisive factor is how much urgency, staff knowledge and the cost of error vary between this firm’s decisions.
Counterargument: must address the real value of consistency to staff.
Condition: must state what would have to be true for varying the style to work - that the rule is explained.

items.prompt: A fuel depot near Walvis Bay employs sixteen tanker drivers, most of them in their first year. Its supervisor sets the loading procedure, the route and the timing, and discusses none of them. Explain why an autocratic style may suit this depot.
items.canonical_answer: Two of the three conditions that favour the style are present in strength. The consequences of a wrong decision are severe: a loading or routing error at a fuel depot risks a fire and the lives of the drivers and anyone nearby, so the supervisor has good reason to refuse to put the method to a vote and to insist it is followed exactly. And the drivers are mostly in their first year, so they have little operating experience to add to the decision and need an unambiguous instruction to do the job safely at all. The style suits the depot’s present circumstances rather than the depot permanently: as those sixteen drivers gain experience the second condition weakens, and the knowledge the supervisor is not asking for becomes worth having.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the depot’s own facts - inexperienced drivers and a safety-critical task.
Reasoning: the conditions that favour the style must be tied to those facts rather than listed in general.
Conclusion: must reach a judgement about this depot; the point that the fit changes as the drivers gain experience is creditable.

items.prompt: Analyse how a persistently autocratic style could raise a business’s costs.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: staff are told rather than asked over a long period, in work where they have knowledge to offer. Mechanism: being consulted is part of what makes people feel valued, so where it is absent the sense of being valued tends to fall, and people who feel undervalued are readier to take a day off and readier to leave for a similar job elsewhere. Consequence: absenteeism rises, which means overtime or agency cover at a higher rate than the absent worker’s own pay, and labour turnover rises, which means recruitment spending, the manager’s time interviewing, and weeks of below-normal output while each replacement is trained. A second route runs alongside: what the people doing the job know never reaches the decision, so avoidable waste and rework continue because nobody in a position to mention them is asked. Effect on an objective: unit cost rises and the margin narrows at an unchanged price. The chain holds where staff have something to contribute and other employers are hiring; where neither is true, the same style may cost very little.
marking_guidance: Condition: the style is sustained over time in work where staff have knowledge to offer.
Mechanism: the route from not being consulted, to a lower sense of being valued, to absence and leaving, must be explicit.
Consequence: must reach measurable costs - cover, recruitment, training time, continued waste.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must end on unit cost or margin, and must carry the condition under which it holds.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of an autocratic style for a business that wants to promote from within.
items.canonical_answer: The limitation is that staff who do not take decisions do not learn to take them. Under an autocratic style the decisions are made by the manager and passed down, so the people below have no practice at weighing options, no experience of being answerable for an outcome, and no record the business could judge them on. When a supervisor’s post falls vacant the business finds it has plenty of people who can do the work and nobody who has been tested at deciding, so it either promotes someone untried or recruits from outside at a higher cost and with a longer settling-in period. The limitation develops over time rather than appearing at once, because what is missing is accumulated practice, and it bites hardest in a business whose senior staff are approaching retirement together.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed to a consequence, not merely named: it has to reach the vacancy the business cannot fill from inside.
Reward the point that the effect builds over time because what is missing is accumulated practice.

items.prompt: A clothing factory in Windhoek faces an export order that must ship in nine days, and its production manager decides to set the whole schedule alone. Evaluate that decision.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: setting the schedule alone is right for this order, but the manager should spend one hour of the nine days consulting the line supervisors before the schedule is fixed. Context: nine days is short enough that a full consultation would eat days the order does not have, and a missed export shipment usually costs the customer as well as the margin on the order. Criterion: the decisive factor is urgency weighed against what consultation would actually add. Urgency here is high, but the supervisors hold the one piece of information the manager cannot get elsewhere - how long each operation really takes on the machines available this week - and that information decides whether the schedule is achievable at all. Counterargument: the strongest case for deciding entirely alone is that a schedule built by committee tends to carry everyone’s safety margin and so promises less than the factory can do. That risk is real, and it is answered by the manager consulting and then deciding, not by refusing to consult. Condition: the judgement would change if the schedule were routine rather than exceptional. A manager who decides alone every week, and not only when nine days are left, is giving up the supervisors’ knowledge permanently and may find them less willing to offer it when it is next needed.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain verdict on this decision is required.
Context: the answer must use the factory’s own facts - nine days and an export shipment.
Criterion: the decisive factor is urgency weighed against what consultation would actually add.
Counterargument: must address the real case for deciding entirely alone.
Condition: must state what would change the judgement, such as the decision being routine rather than exceptional.

items.prompt: Define democratic management.
items.canonical_answer: Democratic management is a style in which the manager consults the people affected and lets their views influence the decision, with communication running both ways. In most businesses the manager still takes the decision and still answers for it; what makes the style democratic is that staff views genuinely change the outcome.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only. The meaning must reach the point that staff views influence the decision.
The boundary that consultation is not the same as a vote is creditable, but no evaluation is required.

items.prompt: Explain one benefit to a business of consulting staff before changing how work is done.
items.canonical_answer: The benefit is that the change is more likely to work, because the people who do the job hold information the manager does not. A supervisor deciding a new bench layout from an office plan does not know that the second bench has to be reached from the left because of where the extraction point sits; the person who works there does. Consulting surfaces that before the layout is fixed, so the business avoids buying the change twice. The benefit develops further at the implementation stage, because staff who helped shape a change tend to carry it out as intended rather than following the letter of the instruction and no further, so the improvement the change was meant to deliver is more likely to appear in the figures. It is largest where the work is complex enough that the manager cannot see all of it, and smallest where the task is simple and fully visible.
marking_guidance: The benefit must be developed to a consequence, not merely named: it has to reach the change working, or the cost of doing it twice.
Reward the condition that the size of the benefit depends on how much the staff know that the manager does not.

items.prompt: A software firm in Windhoek with nine developers must choose between two ways of rebuilding its booking system. Explain why a democratic style is likely to suit this decision.
items.canonical_answer: Because both conditions that make consultation pay are present. The nine developers hold knowledge the manager could not have: which parts of the existing system are fragile, how long each route would really take, and what has already been tried and abandoned. On a question about how the work is done, that knowledge is the main input to a good decision, and a manager choosing without it is guessing. And the people consulted are the people who will do the work, so a route they helped choose is one they are more likely to carry out as designed rather than work around. The decision is also not urgent in the way an emergency is, since a rebuild is planned, so the main cost of the style - its slowness - is small here. The manager still decides and still answers for the choice; what the style changes is whose information is inside it.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the firm’s own facts - nine developers, a technical choice, and no emergency.
Reasoning: both mechanisms must be reached, the information the staff hold and their commitment to carrying it out.
Conclusion: must conclude for this decision, and may note that the slowness of the style costs little here.

items.prompt: Analyse how consulting staff about a change can still leave a business worse off than deciding without them.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the manager consults on a question the staff do not have the information to answer, or consults and then decides against them without explaining why. Mechanism: in the first case the views collected are opinions rather than knowledge, and a manager who weighs them equally with the evidence may choose a worse option than they would have chosen alone, while the consultation also takes time the decision did not have. In the second case, staff who were asked and then overruled without a reason learn that the exercise was for show. Consequence: the decision is worse or later than it needed to be, and the next consultation draws less contribution than this one did, so the information the style exists to reach becomes harder to get. Effect on the business and its staff: the cost of the style is paid and the benefit is not, and trust in what management says falls, which makes later changes harder to introduce. The outcome turns on two things the manager controls - whether the question is one the staff can answer, and whether a decision that goes against them is explained.
marking_guidance: Condition: the consultation is on a question staff cannot answer, or the decision is taken against them with no explanation.
Mechanism: opinion displaces evidence, or the staff learn that the exercise is not real.
Consequence: must reach an observable effect - a worse or later decision, and less contribution next time.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must end on the business or its staff, and must name what the manager controls.

items.prompt: A hospital pharmacy is deciding both its dispensing-error procedure and its shift rota. Evaluate whether its manager should use a democratic style for both.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: democratic for the rota, not for the dispensing-error procedure. Context: this pharmacy holds two decisions of very different kinds in one department - a rota whose consequences the staff themselves bear and whose constraints only they know, and a procedure where a mistake reaches a patient. Criterion: the decisive factor is who bears the consequence of a wrong choice. On the rota it is the staff, so their views are not merely useful but the main evidence. On dispensing errors it is a patient who is not in the room, and the procedure is also likely to be constrained by regulation, so the manager should consult on how a rule is implemented and keep the rule itself. Counterargument: the strongest case for consulting on the procedure too is that the dispensers know where the real errors happen, and a procedure written without them may control the wrong step. That argues for consulting as an input, not for handing over the decision. Condition: the judgement depends on the procedure being one where an error reaches a patient. For an internal stock-recording rule, where a mistake costs money and time but harms nobody, the balance moves back towards the staff deciding.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain verdict is required, and it must separate the two decisions.
Context: the answer must use the pharmacy’s own two decisions rather than arguing about the style in general.
Criterion: the decisive factor is who bears the consequence of a wrong choice.
Counterargument: must address the real value of the dispensers’ knowledge about where errors happen.
Condition: must state what would change the judgement, such as an error that harms nobody.

items.prompt: Define laissez-faire management.
items.canonical_answer: Laissez-faire management is a style in which the manager agrees the objective and then leaves staff to decide for themselves how to achieve it, intervening little.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only. The meaning must include both halves: an objective is agreed, and the method is left to the staff.
No example or evaluation required.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to say that a laissez-faire manager does nothing?
items.canonical_answer: Because the style begins with work the manager has to do. A laissez-faire manager sets or agrees the objective, fixes the deadline and makes the resources available; what is handed over is the method, not the purpose. The manager also stays available and keeps the objective in view, which is why the style is described as intervening little rather than not at all. A manager who has set no objective, agreed no deadline and provided nothing is absent, and an absent manager is not practising a style at all - the difference shows the moment the work goes wrong, because there is nothing to judge it against.
marking_guidance: The answer must say why the belief is wrong, not only that it is: the objective, the deadline and the resources are the manager’s own work.
Reward the distinction between deliberately handing over the method and simply being absent.

items.prompt: A pharmaceutical research group of six scientists is given twelve months and a budget to find a more stable formulation. Explain why a laissez-faire style is likely to suit the group, and what its manager must still do.
items.canonical_answer: It suits them because the work cannot be directed in detail by anybody who is not doing it. The six are specialists, the route to a more stable formulation is not known in advance, and a manager instructing them step by step would be substituting a worse judgement for a better one. Given room, they may try approaches the manager would not have thought of, which is the point of employing them. What the manager must still do is the part that makes it a style rather than absence: the objective is stated as a more stable formulation rather than as research in general, the twelve months is a real deadline, the budget is fixed, and there are check-points at which progress is reviewed. Without those, the group is exposed to exactly the risk the style carries, because twelve months is long enough for work to drift for several of them before anyone notices, and by then the deadline may be beyond recovery.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the group’s own facts - six specialists, an unknown route, and a twelve-month deadline.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that a manager cannot direct work whose method is not known in advance.
Conclusion: must reach both halves - why the style fits, and the objective, deadline and check-points the manager still supplies.

items.prompt: Analyse how a laissez-faire style could damage a business whose work has to be coordinated between teams.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: several teams are each left to choose their own methods, and no check-point brings those choices together. Mechanism: each team settles on what suits its own work, which is what the style invites, but coordination is a property of the joins between teams and no team owns a join. So one team adopts a file format, a component size or a delivery sequence that suits it and does not fit what the next team has built, and because nobody is watching the interface the mismatch is not found until the parts have to meet. Consequence: work already done has to be redone at the point of assembly, which costs materials and paid hours and pushes the completion date out. Effect on an objective and a stakeholder: a deadline each team was individually on course for is missed collectively, and the customer waiting on the assembled result bears the delay. The chain depends on the joins being left unmanaged: a manager who hands over the method inside each team but keeps the interfaces between them removes most of the risk.
marking_guidance: Condition: several teams choose methods independently with no check-point between them.
Mechanism: each team optimises locally while nobody owns the interface between teams.
Consequence: must reach rework, cost and a later completion date.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must end on the deadline and the customer, and must carry the condition that the risk lies in the unmanaged joins.

items.prompt: A design studio of eleven people has grown from three, and its founder still manages it laissez-faire. Evaluate whether the style should change now the studio is larger.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: it should change in part rather than wholly. The founder should keep the style for the design work itself and introduce agreed objectives, deadlines and check-points across the studio. Context: at three people the joins between the work were visible from one desk and everybody knew what the others were doing; at eleven they are not, and a studio of that size almost certainly now has junior staff who did not choose the style and may need guidance the original three never wanted. Criterion: the decisive factor is whether the coordination the style leaves unmanaged is still happening informally. At three it was; at eleven it is unlikely to be, and rework at the joins is what that costs. Counterargument: the strongest case for leaving it alone is that the freedom is why the studio produces the work it does and why its designers stay, and a founder who starts directing method may lose both. That case is answered by separating the two - the method stays with the designers while the objectives and deadlines become explicit - rather than by changing the style across the board. Condition: the judgement depends on whether the junior staff already have somebody supporting them. If experienced designers are in practice coaching them, the studio has replaced what the founder is not doing, and the case for a formal change is weaker.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, and it should say which part changes and which does not.
Context: the answer must use the studio’s own facts - growth from three to eleven, and the junior staff that implies.
Criterion: the decisive factor is whether coordination is still happening informally at the new size.
Counterargument: must address the real case that the freedom is why the work is good and the designers stay.
Condition: must state what would change the judgement, such as senior designers already coaching the juniors.

items.prompt: Define paternalistic management.
items.canonical_answer: Paternalistic management is a style in which the manager takes the decision but explains the reasoning behind it and takes the welfare and interests of staff into account in making it, acting like a parent deciding for a family.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a paternalistic and an autocratic management style.
items.canonical_answer: The difference is not who decides, because both keep the decision with the manager. It is two other things. First, the paternalistic manager explains the reasoning and the autocratic manager need not: an instruction that comes with its reason can be applied by staff to cases the instruction did not cover, while a bare instruction cannot. Second, the paternalistic manager weighs what they judge to be good for the staff as part of making the decision, where the autocratic manager weighs only what is good for the task. A factory closing a shift shows both differences: the autocratic version announces the closure, while the paternalistic version explains why the order book no longer supports the shift and offers the affected staff the first vacancies on the shifts that remain. Neither version has given the staff a say in whether the shift closes.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: the difference lies in explanation and in weighing staff welfare, not in who takes the decision.
Reward the point that neither style gives staff influence over the outcome.

items.prompt: A family-owned abattoir in Gobabis employs thirty people, most of them recruited straight from school and trained on the job. The owner decides everything, explains each decision at a Monday meeting, and runs a transport allowance for staff living outside town. Explain why a paternalistic style may suit this business.
items.canonical_answer: Because the workforce is young and inexperienced, and the owner’s two practices answer what that workforce needs. Staff trained on the job have limited experience to bring to decisions about the business, so the owner keeping those decisions costs the abattoir little in lost knowledge. But people in their first jobs learn faster when they are told why, and a Monday meeting that explains a decision lets them apply the reasoning to situations nobody anticipated - which matters in an abattoir, where hygiene rules cannot cover every case in advance. The transport allowance does the second half of the work: visible concern for a real problem, getting in from outside Gobabis, tends to build loyalty, and staff who stay keep their accumulated experience inside the business. What the style does not give them is a say, and the owner should expect that to become a problem with the ones who stay long enough to know the work better than he does.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the abattoir’s own facts - thirty young staff trained on the job, the Monday explanation, and the transport allowance.
Reasoning: both mechanisms must be tied to those facts - explanation helps inexperienced staff generalise, and visible concern for welfare builds retention.
Conclusion: must conclude for this business; noting the limit that appears as staff gain experience is creditable.

items.prompt: Explain one benefit to a business of explaining a decision to staff rather than simply announcing it.
items.canonical_answer: The benefit is that an explained decision is carried out more accurately, because staff who know the reason can apply it to cases the instruction did not anticipate. A rule that says stock older than thirty days goes back to the supplier tells a storeman what to do with a forty-day box; it tells him nothing about a twenty-day box whose seal is broken. A storeman who has been given the reason - that the business is carrying the cost of stock it cannot sell at full price - can work out that the damaged box goes back too, so the business gets the outcome the rule was written for rather than the letter of it. The benefit develops further where the business is changing often, because each explained decision reduces the number of new instructions a manager has to write. It is smallest where the work is fully prescribed and no case falls outside the rule.
marking_guidance: The benefit must be developed to a consequence, not merely named: it has to reach the decision being carried out correctly in a case the instruction did not anticipate.
Reward the condition that the benefit is largest where cases fall outside the written rule.

items.prompt: Define McGregor’s Theory X.
items.canonical_answer: Theory X is a set of assumptions a manager may hold about people: that the average person dislikes work and avoids it where possible, must therefore be directed, closely supervised and pushed by the threat of penalty, prefers to be told what to do, avoids responsibility, and wants security above everything else.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only. The meaning must say that Theory X is a set of assumptions held by a manager rather than a description of a type of worker.
At least two of the assumptions must be given. No evaluation is required.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between Theory X and Theory Y as McGregor described them.
items.canonical_answer: Both are sets of assumptions a manager holds about people, so the difference lies in what is assumed and not in what kind of worker is being described. Theory X assumes that people dislike work, avoid responsibility, need close supervision and the threat of penalty, and want security above all. Theory Y assumes that effort at work is as natural as rest, that people will direct themselves towards objectives they are committed to, that commitment comes from the satisfaction of achieving something, that people seek responsibility under the right conditions, and that imagination is widely spread in a workforce and largely under-used. The consequence of the difference is practical: the first set leads a manager towards close direction and control, the second towards delegation and self-direction.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: the difference is between two sets of assumptions about people, not between two types of worker.
The consequence of the difference must be stated - what each set leads a manager to do.

items.prompt: Explain how a manager’s Theory X assumptions can produce the very behaviour they assume.
items.canonical_answer: The mechanism is a loop. A manager who assumes people avoid work supervises closely, leaves no discretion and ties effort to penalties. Staff in that position have no opportunity to show initiative, so none is visible. There is no reward for offering an idea, so ideas stop being offered. And people who are watched closely tend to do exactly what is asked and no more, because anything extra is unrewarded and may be criticised. The manager then observes staff doing the minimum and taking no responsibility, and reads it as proof that the assumptions were correct, although the behaviour was produced by the management rather than discovered by it. It is a tendency rather than a certainty: some people behave the same way under any style, and the loop is weaker where staff have alternatives and simply leave instead.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the loop must be traced in order - close supervision, no opportunity, minimum effort, then the manager’s confirmation.
The answer must reach the point that the behaviour was produced by the management, because the opportunity to behave otherwise had been removed.
Reward the qualification that this is a tendency rather than a certainty.

items.prompt: A call centre in Windhoek times every call, scripts every answer and pays a bonus based on penalties for missed targets. Its manager says the staff would do nothing if they were not watched. Explain what McGregor’s framework says about this situation.
items.canonical_answer: The manager is describing Theory X assumptions and has built a workplace that matches them. Scripts remove discretion, timing removes any judgement about when a call needs longer, and a penalty-based bonus ties effort to avoiding punishment rather than to achieving something. McGregor’s point is that the evidence the manager offers cannot settle the question: staff with no discretion have no way of showing initiative, so their not showing any is what the design of the job produces rather than what it reveals about them. The framework does not establish that the manager is wrong about these particular people - some may indeed do little unwatched - but it does show that the call centre has arranged things so that it cannot find out. The test would be to give one team a genuine decision, such as authority to waive a small charge, and see what they do with it.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the call centre’s own facts - the scripts, the timing and the penalty-based bonus.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that the job design removes the opportunity the manager’s evidence would have to come from.
Conclusion: must reach the point that the assumptions are untested here; naming what would test them is creditable.

items.prompt: Evaluate the view that managers do better to hold Theory Y assumptions about their staff than Theory X assumptions.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: for most businesses over time, Theory Y assumptions serve better, but they are a starting position rather than a rule, and a manager who holds them where neither the work nor the staff support them will do damage. Context: the argument matters most in a business employing people whose jobs contain judgement - a workshop, a clinic, a design studio - because that is where the assumptions change what a manager actually does. Criterion: the decisive test is whether staff have the knowledge and experience to use the discretion Theory Y hands them. Where they do, the self-confirming loop runs in the business’s favour: a delegated decision builds capability, capability justifies more delegation, and the business ends with people it can promote. Counterargument: the strongest case for Theory X assumptions is that they are sometimes accurate and that the cost of being wrong is lopsided - handing a safety-critical decision to somebody unready is worse than supervising somebody who did not need it. Condition: the judgement depends on the work and the staff. Where the task is safety-critical, the staff are new, or the deadline is immediate, direction is the right response, and holding Theory Y assumptions does not forbid it, because the assumptions concern what people are capable of rather than what a manager must do this afternoon.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain verdict is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the answer must be argued for work that contains judgement rather than for business in general.
Criterion: the decisive test is whether staff have the knowledge and experience to use the discretion.
Counterargument: must address the real case for Theory X assumptions, including the lopsided cost of being wrong.

items.prompt: A new owner takes over a 30-person engineering workshop and wants to form a view within three months of whether the manager already in post is doing a good job. Identify the questions she should ask about the workshop’s figures and practices before deciding, and explain what each one would tell her.
items.canonical_answer: Is there a plan, and does it carry figures and dates? A plan without them gives the manager nothing to control against, and its absence explains a great deal of what follows. What is compared against the plan, and how often? Weekly comparison means problems are found while they are recoverable; quarterly comparison means they are found when the quarter is already lost. What happened to the last three shortfalls - was a cause found and an action taken? This separates measurement from control, and control is the half that changes anything. What is labour turnover, and how does it compare with the workshop’s own earlier years and with similar workshops in town? Turnover is one of the few indicators a manager plainly influences, and a comparison is what makes a single figure mean anything. What is absenteeism doing? It moves before turnover does, so it is an earlier signal of the same thing. What proportion of jobs left on the promised date? That measures coordination, which nothing else on this list captures. Which decisions does the manager keep, and which are delegated, and does that match how skilled the staff are? A style that fits the workforce is evidence of judgement; one that ignores it is evidence of habit. And finally: how much of last year’s result was set by conditions the manager did not control - a customer lost, an exchange-rate movement, a machine that failed - and how long have the manager’s own decisions had to show? Three months is short next to the lag on training, retention and reorganised workflow, so the owner should expect the practices to be better evidence than the results at this stage.
marking_guidance: State each question plainly before explaining it.
Give the reason each question matters - what a weak answer to it would tell the owner.
Use the context: each question must be answerable from figures or practices the owner of a 30-person workshop can actually see, and the business has had the manager in post for longer than she has.
Reward the point that three months is short relative to the lag on several of these indicators, so practices are better evidence than results.

context.situation: new owner assessing an existing manager
facts: three months to form a view

items.prompt: Kunene Poultry runs two packing halls, each with 60 staff. In Hall A the supervisor sets the line speed and the break pattern and discusses neither; labour turnover in Hall A was 40% last year and each worker packed 32 crates an hour. In Hall B the supervisor agreed the break pattern with the staff and asks them each month what is slowing the line; turnover there was 25% and each worker packed 35 crates an hour. Replacing one packer costs Kunene about N$4 800. Calculate the difference in annual replacement cost between the halls, explain what the packing figures suggest, and evaluate whether Hall A’s supervisor should change style.
items.canonical_answer: Replacements: 40% of 60 staff is 24 people a year in Hall A, and 25% of 60 is 15 in Hall B. The difference is 24 - 15 = 9 replacements, so at N$4 800 each Hall A carries 9 x N$4 800 = N$43 200 a year that Hall B does not. Packing: 35 - 32 = 3 crates an hour per worker, which across 60 workers is 3 x 60 = 180 crates an hour more in Hall B. What the packing figures suggest is the second route by which the styles differ. Hall B’s supervisor asks monthly what is slowing the line, so obstacles the supervisor cannot see get removed; Hall A’s does not ask, so they are not removed. The more experienced workforce that lower turnover leaves behind works in the same direction, since experienced packers make fewer mistakes and lose less time. The figures cannot separate those two effects, and they cannot rule out a third explanation, such as newer equipment in Hall B. Judgement: Hall A’s supervisor should adopt the one practice that is doing the work in Hall B - asking the packers monthly what is slowing the line - rather than converting the hall to a democratic style across the board. Context: N$43 200 a year and 180 crates an hour are Kunene’s own numbers, and they come from two halls doing the same job in the same business, which is the strongest comparison available. Criterion: the decisive factor is that the gap appears on both indicators at once, which is what makes management rather than chance the likely explanation. Counterargument: line speed in a packing hall may be a decision that has to stay with the supervisor for safety and throughput reasons, and a supervisor who starts consulting on everything and then overrules the first answer would leave Hall A worse off than it is now. Condition: the recommendation depends on the two halls being comparable. If Hall A runs older equipment or a different product mix, part of the gap belongs to the equipment and the change of practice will close less of it than the figures imply.
marking_guidance: All three figures must be calculated with working shown: 24 and 15 replacements, the N$43 200 difference, and the 180 crates an hour.
Judgement: the answer must recommend, not set out both halls and stop.
Context: the recommendation must rest on Kunene’s own two halls rather than on the styles in the abstract.
Criterion: the decisive factor is that the gap shows on two independent indicators at once.
Counterargument: must address the case for the supervisor keeping the line-speed decision.
Condition: must name what would weaken the conclusion, such as the halls not being comparable.

context.situation: two comparable halls managed in different styles
facts: Hall A turnover 40%, 32 crates an hour per worker
Hall B turnover 25%, 35 crates an hour per worker

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Namib Analytics employs 22 data scientists on client projects. Its new head of department believes people work best when left alone and intends to manage the whole department laissez-faire. Evaluate whether that is the right approach.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement to reach: right for the analysis work inside each project, wrong as a department-wide approach, because client deadlines and the joins between projects need objectives and check-points the style does not supply. Paragraph 1 - what makes the style plausible here: 22 specialists whose methods the head cannot direct in detail, work where the route is not known in advance, and staff likely to value the freedom. Paragraph 2 - what the head’s stated belief actually is: a set of Theory Y assumptions, which the department may well justify, but the assumptions describe what people are capable of rather than what the department needs managing. Paragraph 3 - the mechanism that breaks: client work runs to dates the client sets, and 22 people choosing their own priorities separately leaves the joins between projects unowned, so drift is found at delivery rather than during the work. Paragraph 4 - the strongest case against changing anything: introducing close direction would remove the freedom that attracts and keeps data scientists, and a head who starts directing method is substituting a worse judgement for a better one. Judgement and condition: keep the method with the scientists, make objectives, deadlines and check-points explicit at department level, and revisit if the department turns out to contain juniors who need more than that. The answer changes if the 22 are all experienced and the projects genuinely do not touch each other.
marking_guidance: A plan is what is assessed, not an essay: structure with a stated judgement.
Judgement: the plan must show where the recommendation is reached.
Context: the plan must use Namib Analytics’ own facts - 22 data scientists, client projects, a new head.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be the coordination and deadlines the style leaves unmanaged.
Counterargument: must include the real case for leaving the specialists alone.
Condition: must end on what would change the answer, such as the seniority of the staff or projects that do not touch each other.

context.situation: new department head intending one style for everybody
facts: head believes people work best alone

items.prompt: Ongwediva Steel has grown from 20 to 95 employees in four years. Its founder still takes every decision, spends his days dealing with whatever has gone wrong, and has not written a plan since the business started. A consultant tells him he has stopped managing. Analyse what Fayol’s functions and Mintzberg’s roles each reveal about the founder’s working day, and evaluate what he should change first.
items.canonical_answer: Mintzberg’s roles describe the day accurately and, read on their own, make it look normal. Dealing with whatever has gone wrong is the disturbance-handler role, taking every decision makes him the resource allocator for 95 people, and a founder of a growing steel business is doing plenty of negotiating. Fragmentation and reactive work are what Mintzberg found in managers generally, so the consultant cannot be right that the founder has stopped working. What the roles do show is the shape of the distortion: the entrepreneur and monitor roles have almost disappeared, and those are the two that are not forced on a manager by events. Fayol’s functions show what that costs, because they name the purposes rather than the activities. Forecasting and planning is absent - no plan in four years, during which the business has grown by a factor of nearly five. Controlling is absent as a consequence, because there is nothing to compare results against, so the founder cannot know whether 95 employees are producing proportionately more than 20 were. Coordinating is the function under most strain, since a business that size cannot be held in step by one person reacting. Only commanding is fully served, and organising only partly, since the decisions have not been delegated as the headcount has grown. Recommendation: he should change organising first, by delegating a defined set of decisions to two or three supervisors, and then put a simple monthly plan and comparison in place. The decisive factor is that planning and controlling both need time he does not currently have, and delegation is the only one of the three that creates time rather than consuming it. The strongest argument against starting there is risk: decisions delegated to supervisors who have never taken one will produce mistakes, and in a steel works some mistakes are expensive or dangerous. That argues for delegating a defined list and keeping the safety-critical decisions, not for keeping everything. The recommendation depends on there being supervisors capable of being developed; if there are not, recruiting one experienced supervisor comes first, and the delegation follows.
marking_guidance: Both frameworks must be applied to the founder’s day before the recommendation is made.
Judgement: a recommendation naming what he should change first is required.
Context: must use Ongwediva Steel’s own facts - growth from 20 to 95, no plan in four years, every decision kept.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be that delegation creates the time the other two functions need.
Counterargument: must address the risk of delegating to supervisors who have never taken a decision.
Condition: must state what the recommendation depends on, such as whether supervisors capable of being developed already exist.

context.situation: founder-managed business that has outgrown its management
facts: grown from 20 to 95 employees in four years
no written plan in four years
